item.title: Simulating Bulletproofs Under Adaptive Corruptions
item.dc:creator: Paul Gerhart
item.description: We show how to reconstruct consistent prover randomness given a simulated Bulletproof and a valid witness for the proof's statement.
item.content:encoded:
A zero-knowledge proof [GMR85] allows a prover to convince a verifier that a public statement x\stmtx of an NP-relation is true without revealing the corresponding witness w\witw. For example, x\stmtx may be a public key x=gw\stmt=g^\witx=gw, where ggg generates a group of prime order ppp and w\witw is the secret key. A zero-knowledge proof could then convince the verifier that the prover knows the secret key, without revealing any information besides the already known public key x\stmtx. In this post, we focus on non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs, or NIZKs [BFM88], which allow the prover to generate such a proof π\piπ without interacting with the verifier.

In cryptography, we formalize the promise that a proof “reveals no additional information” through simulation. We say a proof is zero-knowledge if an efficient algorithm (called a simulator) that only knows a statement x\stmtx but does not know the witness w\witw can produce valid proofs that no efficient verifier can distinguish from honest proofs. Whatever the verifier learns from an honest proof, it could then also have learned from a simulated proof, which carries no information about the witness to begin with.

At first glance, this seems paradoxical. If a simulator can produce valid proofs without knowing the witness, why should a proof convince a verifier? The simulator has access to a trapdoor, a piece of secret information that lets it produce proofs without the witness. At the same time, no real prover has access to the trapdoor, so proofs from a real prover are sound (can only be computed when knowing a valid witness). For Fiat–Shamir-based proofs [FS86], which are the subject of this post, the simulator’s trapdoor is the power to program the random oracle [BR93], which is not possible with a real hash function.

This simulation property is useful when proving the security of a larger protocol, where NIZKs are used as a building block. Throughout the security proof of such a higher-level protocol, the reduction can first use the NIZK’s simulator to generate proofs without knowing a valid witness, and then embed a challenge element in the NIZK’s statement. With our example NIZK of secret-key knowledge, this would allow the reduction to embed a discrete-logarithm (DLog) challenge element into the public key while still producing accepting proofs of knowledge of the secret key. If the adversary breaks the modified protocol, the reduction uses this break to compute the discrete logarithm of the embedded element. Since replacing honest proofs with simulated ones results in an indistinguishable view for the adversary, any adversary that breaks the real protocol can also be used to break the modified protocol, which in turn allows solving DLog. Because DLog is assumed to be hard, no such adversary can exist.

This proof technique is standard in cryptographic literature and yields secure higher-level protocols under static corruptions, where the adversary chooses which parties to corrupt before the protocol starts. Under static corruptions, the reduction only needs to simulate the remaining honest parties. These parties stay uncorrupted throughout the execution, so the reduction never has to reveal the internal state behind their simulated proofs. For this part of the security argument, producing indistinguishable proofs is sufficient.

In practice, however, adversaries do not usually decide before a protocol starts which parties they will eventually corrupt. To model this, cryptographers use adaptive corruptions [CGJKR99], where the adversary can choose parties to corrupt during the execution of a protocol, based on the protocol messages it has already seen. If the adversary decides to corrupt such a party, then the reduction has to provide all secret information in the state of this party (including all the randomness used so far). The gap between static and adaptive corruptions might seem small at first sight, but adaptive corruptions have a big impact on the way we can do security proofs. For example, an adversary could wait until all honest parties have published a NIZK, and then decide to corrupt a random party.

Even if this does not help the adversary break the protocol, it complicates our proof. If we want to use the proof strategy discussed above, we cannot simply replace all honest proofs by simulated ones, since the reduction has to reveal the randomness behind a simulated proof as soon as its prover is corrupted. The adversary can check that this randomness is consistent with the public transcript by running the honest prover again. A simulated proof, however, was produced without the witness, and the random choices of the simulator need not be valid randomness for the honest prover. Even if the witness becomes available upon corruption, the proof is already fixed and cannot be replaced. Thus, indistinguishability of the proof alone no longer suffices.

There are three ways around this problem. First, the reduction can guess in advance which parties the adversary will corrupt. It then computes the proofs of these parties honestly (it knows their witnesses, since it embeds the challenge only in the statements of the others) and simulates the remaining proofs. If the guess turns out to be wrong, the reduction aborts. For a single corruption among nnn parties, this costs a factor of nnn in the success probability of the reduction, which is still polynomial. Threshold protocols, however, allow the adversary to corrupt up to ttt of the nnn parties, and if it corrupts ttt of them at random, a guess of this set is correct only with probability 1/(nt)1/\binom{n}{t}1/(tn​). For n=100n=100n=100 and t=50t=50t=50, the reduction loses a factor larger than 2962^{96}296 in its success probability.

Second, honest parties can use secure erasures [CGJKR99] and delete the randomness of a proof directly after sending it. A later corruption then no longer reveals this randomness. This, however, is an additional assumption on how honest parties are implemented.

Third, the reduction can simulate all proofs anyway and, once the witness becomes available upon corruption, try to reconstruct randomness that makes the honest prover output exactly the proof it already published. For this post we can simply assume that the reduction obtains a valid witness for the statement of a corrupted party, since upon corruption the reduction must hand over the witness as part of the party’s state anyway.

Reconstructing the prover’s state#

We take the third approach, since we want to avoid assuming secure erasures and cannot efficiently guess which parties the adversary will corrupt. This means that we want to reconstruct randomness for a simulated proof given a valid witness.

If a reduction is able to reconstruct the prover’s state behind a simulated proof, this fixes the gap in the sketched adaptive security proof of the higher-level protocol. Throughout the security proof of the higher-level protocol, the reduction can again first use the NIZK’s simulator to generate proofs without knowing a valid witness, and then embed a challenge element in the NIZK’s statement. When the adversary corrupts a party, the reduction obtains this party’s witness, uses it to reconstruct the randomness behind every proof the party has published, and returns this randomness as part of the party’s internal state.

To make this simulation strategy undetectable to the adversary, the reconstructed randomness has to satisfy two requirements. It must make the honest prover reproduce exactly the proof that was published, and it must be distributed like the randomness of an honest prover.

We formalize this property as honest prover state reconstruction, following Groth, Ostrovsky and Sahai [GOS06].

Definition 1 (Honest prover state reconstruction).

Let Π=(Prove,Verify)\Pi=(\mathrm{Prove},\mathrm{Verify})Π=(Prove,Verify) be a NIZK for a relation R\mathcal RR in the random oracle model, where Prove\mathrm{Prove}Prove takes its randomness rrr as an explicit input and every public parameter is derived from the random oracle HHH. Then Π\PiΠ has honest prover state reconstruction if there are efficient algorithms Sim\mathrm{Sim}Sim and Rec\mathrm{Rec}Rec with a shared state st\mathrm{st}st such that for every efficient adversary A\mathcal AA

Pr⁡[AH, Oreal=1]≈Pr⁡[ASim, Osim=1], \Pr\bigl[\mathcal A^{H,\,\mathcal O_{\mathrm{real}}}=1\bigr] \approx \Pr\bigl[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{Sim},\,\mathcal O_{\mathrm{sim}}}=1\bigr], Pr[AH,Oreal​=1]≈Pr[ASim,Osim​=1],

where HHH is a random function in the first experiment and Sim\mathrm{Sim}Sim answers the adversary’s random-oracle queries in the second. Both oracles take a pair (x,w)(\stmt,\wit)(x,w), return ⊥\bot⊥ if (x,w)∉R(\stmt,\wit)\notin\mathcal R(x,w)∈/R, and otherwise answer as follows.

  • Oreal(x,w)\mathcal O_{\mathrm{real}}(\stmt,\wit)Oreal​(x,w) samples rrr, computes π←ProveH(x,w;r)\pi\gets\mathrm{Prove}^{H}(\stmt,\wit;r)π←ProveH(x,w;r), and returns (π,r)(\pi,r)(π,r).
  • Osim(x,w)\mathcal O_{\mathrm{sim}}(\stmt,\wit)Osim​(x,w) lets Sim\mathrm{Sim}Sim compute a proof π\piπ on input x\stmtx, programming its random oracle as needed, then computes r←Rec(st,x,w)r\gets\mathrm{Rec}(\mathrm{st},\stmt,\wit)r←Rec(st,x,w), and returns (π,r)(\pi,r)(π,r).

Note that in the simulated experiment the witness reaches only Rec\mathrm{Rec}Rec, after Sim\mathrm{Sim}Sim has already fixed the proof, which is what happens in our sketched security proof upon a corruption. For Fiat–Shamir proofs, the adversary re-runs the prover against the same random oracle, so the randomness has to reproduce the proof under the answers the simulator programmed. We also allow the reconstruction algorithm to use the simulator’s retained state, which includes every random-oracle answer the simulator chose, and ask it to reconstruct randomness only for proofs that this simulator produced.

State reconstruction for Schnorr proofs#

The goal of this post is to show that Bulletproofs have honest prover state reconstruction. As a warm-up, we first recall honest prover state reconstruction for Schnorr proofs [Sch91], as observed by Bacho et al. [BLSW24]. We return to our example of proving knowledge of the secret key w\witw for a public key x=gw\stmt=g^\witx=gw. Recall that to compute such a Schnorr proof, the prover samples a random element r←$Zpr\sample\ZZ_pr$​Zp​, sends A=grA=g^rA=gr, and answers the challenge c=H(x,A)c=H(\stmt,A)c=H(x,A) with z=r+cwz=r+c\witz=r+cw. To simulate such a proof, the simulator samples (c,z)←$Zp2(c,z) \sample \ZZ_p^2(c,z)$​Zp2​ uniformly and sets A=gzx−cA=g^z\stmt^{-c}A=gzx−c, which satisfies the verification equation gz=Axcg^z=A\stmt^cgz=Axc. It then programs the random oracle to return ccc on input (x,A)(\stmt,A)(x,A), provided that this input has not already been queried.

Theorem 1 (Schnorr proofs have honest prover state reconstruction).

Schnorr’s proof of knowledge of a discrete logarithm has honest prover state reconstruction in the sense of Definition 1.

Proof (Reconstructing the Schnorr prover's randomness).

We construct an algorithm Rec\mathrm{Rec}Rec that, given the simulator’s state (c,z)(c,z)(c,z) and the witness w\witw, computes

r=z−cw(modp). r=z-c\wit\pmod p. r=z−cw(modp).

Since x=gw\stmt=g^\witx=gw, this gives gr=gzx−c=Ag^r=g^z\stmt^{-c}=Agr=gzx−c=A, and the honest prover’s response is r+cw=zr+c\wit=zr+cw=z, so re-running the prover on rrr against the programmed oracle reproduces π\piπ. In the real experiment rrr is uniform and the challenge c=H(x,A)c=H(\stmt,A)c=H(x,A) is uniform and independent of it. In the simulated experiment ccc and zzz are uniform and independent, and for fixed ccc and w\witw subtracting cwc\witcw is a bijection, so ccc and rrr are uniform and independent as well. Both experiments therefore give the same joint distribution of π\piπ and rrr, unless Sim\mathrm{Sim}Sim has to program a point (x,A)(\stmt,A)(x,A) that is already defined. Let the adversary make qHq_HqH​ random-oracle queries and qPq_PqP​ proof queries. Since AAA is uniform in a group of order ppp, a single proof hits an already defined point with probability at most (qH+qP)/p(q_H+q_P)/p(qH​+qP​)/p, and a union bound over the qPq_PqP​ proofs shows that the two experiments differ by at most qP(qH+qP)/pq_P(q_H+q_P)/pqP​(qH​+qP​)/p, which is negligible in the security parameter.

The same argument applies to other Schnorr-type proofs whose responses are linear in the witness, such as proofs of equality of discrete logarithms or of knowledge of a Pedersen opening, where the reconstruction algorithm subtracts the challenge times the witness from each response.

For Schnorr proofs, honest prover state reconstruction is possible, so they can be simulated in adaptive protocols without assuming secure erasures upon corruption. However, a Schnorr proof sends one response per secret value, so the proof size grows linearly with the witness. To make protocols that use NIZKs for large witnesses more efficient, one can use Bulletproofs [BBB+18] instead of Schnorr proofs. In contrast to Schnorr proofs, Bulletproofs grow only logarithmically in the witness size, but like Schnorr proofs, they need no trusted setup and rely only on the discrete-logarithm assumption.

Pedersen commitments#

Before we turn to Bulletproofs, we need one more building block, namely Pedersen commitments [Ped91]. Intuitively, a commitment scheme works like a sealed envelope. In the commit phase, a committer puts a value mmm into the envelope and hands it to a receiver, who cannot look inside. In the opening phase, the committer reveals mmm, and the receiver checks it against the value sealed in the envelope. Proof systems use commitments to let the prover fix a value before it sees the verifier’s challenge, without revealing it yet.

To compute a Pedersen commitment to a single value, we need a second generator hhh of our group. To commit to m∈Zpm\in\ZZ_pm∈Zp​, the committer samples a random ρ←$Zp\rho\sample\ZZ_pρ$​Zp​ and sends C=gmhρC=g^mh^\rhoC=gmhρ. To open the commitment, it reveals mmm and ρ\rhoρ, and the receiver checks that C=gmhρC=g^mh^\rhoC=gmhρ.

A commitment should satisfy two properties. First, it should be hiding, which means that CCC reveals no information about mmm. For Pedersen commitments, this holds since for every pair of values m≠m′m \neq m'm=m′ and every ρ\rhoρ, there is exactly one ρ′\rho'ρ′ with gmhρ=gm′hρ′g^mh^\rho=g^{m'}h^{\rho'}gmhρ=gm′hρ′. Every commitment could thus equally well contain any other value, and since ρ\rhoρ is uniformly random, CCC has the same distribution no matter which value it contains. Second, it should be binding, which means that the committer cannot open CCC to a different value later. If it could, it would know two openings (m,ρ)(m,\rho)(m,ρ) and (m′,ρ′)(m',\rho')(m′,ρ′) with m≠m′m\neq m'm=m′ and gmhρ=gm′hρ′g^mh^\rho=g^{m'}h^{\rho'}gmhρ=gm′hρ′, from which it could compute the discrete logarithm log⁡hg=(ρ′−ρ)/(m−m′)\log_h g=(\rho'-\rho)/(m-m')logh​g=(ρ′−ρ)/(m−m′). Pedersen commitments are thus binding as long as the discrete-logarithm assumption between ggg and hhh holds.

On the other hand, Pedersen commitments are equivocable. This means that anyone who knows ν=log⁡hg\nu=\log_h gν=logh​g can compute the randomness ρ′=ρ+ν(m−m′)\rho'=\rho+\nu(m-m')ρ′=ρ+ν(m−m′) from the hiding property, and thus open a commitment C=gmhρC=g^mh^\rhoC=gmhρ to any other value m′m'm′. We call ν\nuν the trapdoor of the commitment. Just like the simulator’s trapdoor for proofs, this trapdoor will become important later. Pedersen commitments also let us commit to whole vectors m∈Zpn\mathbf m\in\ZZ_p^nm∈Zpn​ at once in a single group element. This works by using one generator per entry via C=hρ∏igimiC=h^\rho\prod_ig_i^{m_i}C=hρ∏i​gimi​​. Such a vector commitment is binding as long as nobody knows a discrete-logarithm relation between the generators, and anyone who knows the discrete logarithms of all generators to the base hhh can again open it to any vector. To make sure that a security reduction can know such a relation while real protocol participants do not, one typically derives all generators through the random oracle by hashing public labels [BBB+18].

Bulletproofs#

At their core, Bulletproofs use an inner-product argument, which proves that two committed vectors have a given inner product. More formally, for generators g=(g1,…,gn)\mathbf g=(g_1,\ldots,g_n)g=(g1​,…,gn​), h=(h1,…,hn)\mathbf h=(h_1,\ldots,h_n)h=(h1​,…,hn​) and uuu, and writing ga=∏igiai\mathbf g^{\mathbf a}=\prod_i g_i^{a_i}ga=∏i​giai​​, the prover of an inner-product argument shows that it knows vectors a,b∈Zpn\mathbf a,\mathbf b\in\ZZ_p^na,b∈Zpn​ with P=gahbu⟨a,b⟩P=\mathbf g^{\mathbf a}\mathbf h^{\mathbf b}u^{\langle\mathbf a,\mathbf b\rangle}P=gahbu⟨a,b⟩ for a public group element PPP. Inner-product arguments are useful for NIZKs because many statements can be expressed as inner products. Evaluating a committed polynomial with coefficient vector a\mathbf aa at a point zzz, for instance, is the inner product ⟨a,(1,z,…,zn−1)⟩\langle\mathbf a,(1,z,\ldots,z^{n-1})\rangle⟨a,(1,z,…,zn−1)⟩, and the constraints of an arithmetic circuit can be checked all at once through a random linear combination that collapses them into a single inner product [BCC+16].

To prove an inner product without sending 2n2n2n field elements, Bulletproofs use the split-and-fold technique of [BCC+16, BBB+18]. It splits both vectors into halves a1,a2\mathbf a_1,\mathbf a_2a1​,a2​ and b1,b2\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2b1​,b2​ and, for a challenge xxx, folds them into a′=xa1+x−1a2\mathbf a'=x\mathbf a_1+x^{-1}\mathbf a_2a′=xa1​+x−1a2​ and b′=x−1b1+xb2\mathbf b'=x^{-1}\mathbf b_1+x\mathbf b_2b′=x−1b1​+xb2​ of half the length, whose inner product is ⟨a′,b′⟩=⟨a,b⟩+x2⟨a1,b2⟩+x−2⟨a2,b1⟩\langle\mathbf a',\mathbf b'\rangle=\langle\mathbf a,\mathbf b\rangle+x^2\langle\mathbf a_1,\mathbf b_2\rangle+x^{-2}\langle\mathbf a_2,\mathbf b_1\rangle⟨a′,b′⟩=⟨a,b⟩+x2⟨a1​,b2​⟩+x−2⟨a2​,b1​⟩. The folded vectors thus satisfy the same relation once the two cross terms ⟨a1,b2⟩\langle\mathbf a_1,\mathbf b_2\rangle⟨a1​,b2​⟩ and ⟨a2,b1⟩\langle\mathbf a_2,\mathbf b_1\rangle⟨a2​,b1​⟩ are accounted for. To account for these cross terms, the prover computes the two group elements L=g2a1h1b2u⟨a1,b2⟩L=\mathbf g_2^{\mathbf a_1}\mathbf h_1^{\mathbf b_2}u^{\langle\mathbf a_1,\mathbf b_2\rangle}L=g2a1​​h1b2​​u⟨a1​,b2​⟩ and R=g1a2h2b1u⟨a2,b1⟩R=\mathbf g_1^{\mathbf a_2}\mathbf h_2^{\mathbf b_1}u^{\langle\mathbf a_2,\mathbf b_1\rangle}R=g1a2​​h2b1​​u⟨a2​,b1​⟩.

Given the two group elements LLL and RRR, both parties can fold the generators to half the length and set P′=Lx2PRx−2P'=L^{x^2}PR^{x^{-2}}P′=Lx2PRx−2, whose extra factors add exactly the two cross terms. Because Fiat–Shamir derives xxx only after LLL and RRR are fixed, the prover cannot choose them to hide a wrong inner product. The result P′P'P′ is again an instance of the same relation, but of half the length. To proceed, the prover applies this step recursively, until after log⁡2n\log_2 nlog2​n rounds each vector is a single scalar. With this technique, the proof consists of 2log⁡2n2\log_2 n2log2​n group elements and two scalars. Apart from a\mathbf aa and b\mathbf bb this prover uses no randomness.

The protocol we have described so far is not zero-knowledge, since PPP and the final scalars are functions of the vectors. To make it zero-knowledge, Bulletproofs+ [CHJ+22] use the hiding property of Pedersen commitments and add a random power of hhh to every group element. (Bulletproofs+ actually prove weighted inner products, but for this post we set all weights to 111.) First, the statement itself becomes a hiding commitment P=gahbu⟨a,b⟩hαP=\mathbf g^{\mathbf a}\mathbf h^{\mathbf b}u^{\langle\mathbf a,\mathbf b\rangle}h^{\alpha}P=gahbu⟨a,b⟩hα with a random blinding exponent α\alphaα. Then, in every round, the prover samples two fresh exponents dL,dR←$Zpd_L,d_R\sample\ZZ_pdL​,dR​$​Zp​ and sends the blinded cross terms

Folding works as before, but the prover additionally keeps track of the blinding exponent of the folded commitment P′=Lx2PRx−2P'=L^{x^2}PR^{x^{-2}}P′=Lx2PRx−2, which is α′=α+x2dL+x−2dR\alpha'=\alpha+x^2d_L+x^{-2}d_Rα′=α+x2dL​+x−2dR​.

In the last round, where the prover would otherwise send the scalars aaa and bbb in the clear, it now proves that it knows aaa, bbb and α\alphaα with a Schnorr-like step. It samples r,s,δ,η←$Zpr,s,\delta,\eta\sample\ZZ_pr,s,δ,η$​Zp​, sends the two commitments

Just like in a Schnorr proof, the random rrr and sss hide aaa and bbb in the responses. The verifier then checks that Pe2AeB=g∗r′eh∗s′eur′s′hδ′P^{e^2}A^eB=g_\ast^{r'e}h_\ast^{s'e}u^{r's'}h^{\delta'}Pe2AeB=g∗r′e​h∗s′e​ur′s′hδ′, where AAA and BBB provide the cross terms rb+sarb+sarb+sa and rsrsrs that show up in ur′s′u^{r's'}ur′s′.

Put together, the Bulletproof inner-product argument for vectors of length nnn consists of the blinded cross terms of all k=log⁡2nk=\log_2 nk=log2​n rounds and the messages of the final Schnorr-like step,

π=(L1,R1,…,Lk,Rk,A,B,r′,s′,δ′). \pi=(L_1,R_1,\ldots,L_k,R_k,A,B,r',s',\delta'). π=(L1​,R1​,…,Lk​,Rk​,A,B,r′,s′,δ′).

With Fiat–Shamir, the challenge xjx_jxj​ of round jjj and the last challenge eee are hashes of PPP and all previous messages, so the verifier can recompute them from π\piπ and fold the generators and PPP itself.

With these changes, we get a zero-knowledge argument that the prover knows a\mathbf aa, b\mathbf bb and α\alphaα with P=gahbu⟨a,b⟩hαP=\mathbf g^{\mathbf a}\mathbf h^{\mathbf b}u^{\langle\mathbf a,\mathbf b\rangle}h^{\alpha}P=gahbu⟨a,b⟩hα. Compared to the plain argument, it costs only two more group elements and one more scalar. The original Bulletproofs [BBB+18] make the argument zero-knowledge in a different way, by running it on randomly masked vectors. In this post we focus on the approach of Bulletproofs+, and come back to the original one in Corollary 1.

Simulating Bulletproofs#

To simulate Bulletproofs without knowing a valid witness, the simulator can follow a strategy similar to the one for Schnorr proofs. In the rounds of the argument, the simulator samples every LLL and RRR as a uniformly random group element. These are distributed exactly like the blinded cross terms of an honest prover. The round challenges come from the random oracle as usual. For the last step, the simulator samples the responses r′,s′,δ′r',s',\delta'r′,s′,δ′ and the challenge eee uniformly, together with a random group element BBB, and then computes AAA such that the verification equation holds. Finally, as in the Schnorr simulation, the simulator programs the random oracle to return eee on the transcript ending with AAA and BBB, provided that this input has not already been queried.

Let us now try to reconstruct the prover’s randomness for such a simulated proof, once we know the witness a\mathbf aa, b\mathbf bb and α\alphaα. We do this in the opposite order in which the simulator computed the proof. For the last step, we can apply the Schnorr trick from above, computing r=r′−aer=r'-aer=r′−ae and s=s′−bes=s'-bes=s′−be. For the blinding exponents, however, we run into a problem. Since the simulator sampled LLL as a random group element, we need a dLd_LdL​ for which the honest prover would have sent the same LLL, namely

hdL=L g2−a1h1−b2u−⟨a1,b2⟩. h^{d_L}=L\,\mathbf g_2^{-\mathbf a_1}\mathbf h_1^{-\mathbf b_2}u^{-\langle\mathbf a_1,\mathbf b_2\rangle}. hdL​=Lg2−a1​​h1−b2​​u−⟨a1​,b2​⟩.

The same holds for dRd_RdR​ in every round and for η\etaη in BBB. Finding such a dLd_LdL​ means computing a discrete logarithm. However, it can also be found with the trapdoor of the Pedersen commitments involved, which consists of the discrete logarithms of all generators to the base hhh.

Our simulator can obtain this trapdoor because the generators come from the random oracle. In the simulated experiment of Definition 1, the simulator answers all random-oracle queries itself, so it also decides what the generators are. It answers the query for hhh honestly, but every other generator query with hθh^{\theta}hθ for a fresh uniform exponent θ\thetaθ. Since hθh^\thetahθ is again a uniformly random group element, the adversary cannot notice this change. This way, the simulator knows scalars κ,λ,ν,ω\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\lambda,\nu,\omegaκ,λ,ν,ω with

gi=hκi,hi=hλi,g=hν,u=hω, g_i=h^{\kappa_i},\qquad h_i=h^{\lambda_i},\qquad g=h^{\nu},\qquad u=h^{\omega}, gi​=hκi​,hi​=hλi​,g=hν,u=hω,

which we call the generator trapdoor. Once the simulator knows the generator trapdoor, it also knows the discrete logarithms of all folded generators, since folding only raises the generators to known powers of the challenges and multiplies them. For example, log⁡hgi′=x−1κi+x κi+n/2\log_h g'_i=x^{-1}\kappa_i+x\,\kappa_{i+n/2}logh​gi′​=x−1κi​+xκi+n/2​. In the same way, it samples every LLL, RRR and BBB as a power of hhh and remembers the exponents, which we denote by θL\theta_LθL​, θR\theta_RθR​ and θB\theta_BθB​. Note that this needs no additional assumption, since the simulator already programs the random oracle for the Fiat–Shamir challenges.

Using the trapdoor in a larger protocol#

If a security proof relies on the generator trapdoor, it can no longer rely on the binding property of the Pedersen commitments, since the reduction can equivocate the commitments. If the surrounding protocol needs binding, its security proof therefore has to establish binding before it switches to the generator trapdoor. This adds two experiments to the sequence from the introduction, which sit between the honest execution and the experiment with simulated NIZK proofs.

In the first experiment, the random oracle still answers the generator queries honestly, but the experiment aborts as soon as the adversary opens a commitment to two different values. This experiment differs from the honest execution only if the abort happens. An adversary that causes an abort reveals a discrete-logarithm relation between the honest generators, an event with negligible probability under DLog.

In the second experiment, the random oracle answers the generator queries with powers of hhh whose exponents the reduction knows. This switch does not change the distribution of the generators, so the adversary cannot distinguish the second experiment from the first. From now on, the reduction no longer needs binding, since every binding break already leads to an abort. Extraction from adversarial Bulletproofs [GOP+22, DG23] is unaffected, because the adversary never learns the trapdoor.

From inner products to range proofs and arithmetic circuits#

So far, we have reconstructed the randomness of the inner-product argument itself. For a full range proof or arithmetic-circuit proof, we also need to reconstruct the randomness used in the commitments and masking steps around that argument. We start with the range proof of Bulletproofs+, then turn to the masked-vector construction used in the original Bulletproofs.

Corollary 1 (Range proofs and arithmetic circuits).

The range proofs of Bulletproofs+ [CHJ+22] and of Bulletproofs [BBB+18], as well as the arithmetic-circuit protocol of Bulletproofs, made non-interactive with Fiat–Shamir and with generators derived from the random oracle, have honest prover state reconstruction in the sense of Definition 1.

Conclusion#

Simulating NIZK proofs is a standard step in security proofs, but it becomes much harder once the adversary can corrupt parties adaptively. Upon a corruption, the reduction has to reveal the randomness behind every proof of the corrupted party, including the proofs that it simulated without a witness. Since guessing the corrupted parties in advance is too costly in general, the reduction either relies on secure erasures or has to reconstruct randomness that is consistent with the simulated proofs. For Schnorr proofs, this reconstruction was already established and takes a single subtraction, but for Bulletproofs it was left as an open problem [BLSW24].

In this post, we showed that Bulletproofs have honest prover state reconstruction, both the zero-knowledge argument of Bulletproofs+ [CHJ+22] and the range proof and circuit protocol of the original Bulletproofs [BBB+18]. The key observation is that every group element that the prover blinds is a Pedersen commitment, and the remaining group elements follow from the verification equations or from a deterministic computation on values that are already fixed. A simulator that programs the generators through the random oracle knows their discrete logarithms and can therefore open each blinded commitment to the witness it learns upon corruption. Protocols that simulate Bulletproofs in their security proof therefore no longer need to assume secure erasures for the randomness of these proofs.
